```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.4, dpi = 90)
library(varm)
library(ggplot2)
Y <- as.matrix(yraw)  # infl, unemp, rate
have <- function(pkg) requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)
sci <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "e", digits = 1)
```

This report states what was checked, against what, and how close the numbers
are. Checks are of three kinds:

* **Exact agreement** with an independent implementation (`vars`, `BVAR`,
  `lpirfs`, `lm` + `sandwich`, closed-form or quadrature results). These run
  live in this document (section 2), so the numbers below are recomputed
  every time the vignette is built.
* **Statistical agreement** (Monte Carlo error, Geweke joint-distribution
  tests, simulation-based calibration, coverage simulations). These take
  minutes, so section 3 *quotes* the output of the scripts in `validation/`,
  with the exact command that reproduces each block.
* **Known failures and limitations** found by those checks (section 5). They
  are listed because a validation report that only shows passes is not
  informative.

Numbers quoted in section 3 and 4 were produced on an Apple M4 Pro, R 4.6.1,
macOS 26.6, OpenBLAS, with the version of the code in this repository. They are
single runs with the seeds in the scripts; Monte Carlo errors are noted where
they matter.

## 1. How to run everything

From the package root:

```sh
# unit tests (65 tests, 728 expectations; about 17 s)
Rscript validation/run-all.R                    # same as testthat::test_dir("tests/testthat")

# heavier validation scripts (not run by run-all.R)
Rscript validation/bayes.R                      # sections s1-s8 and s2d, about 3 min
Rscript validation/bayes.R s5 s7                # a subset of sections
Rscript validation/ident-extra.R                # about 5 s
Rscript validation/proxy-bayes-full.R           # reps T (default 50, 300), about 5 s
Rscript validation/proxy-coverage.R 200 199 200 # reps nboot T, about 5 s
Rscript validation/lp-extra.R                   # about 10 s
Rscript validation/tvp.R                        # about 4 min
```

`validation/run-all.R` runs only `tests/testthat`. The scripts in `validation/`
print `[PASS]`/`[FAIL]` lines (`bayes.R`) or raw numbers for inspection (the
others); they are not wired into `R CMD check`. The reference packages are
listed under `Suggests`; tests that need one skip when it is missing
(`svars` is listed but not installed on the machine used here, and no check in
this report uses it).

At the time of writing the test suite gives
65 tests / 728 expectations / 0 failures / 0 skips (about 17 s), over ten files:

| file | covers |
|---|---|
| `test-var.R` | OLS, `logLik`, IC, stability, Cholesky IRF/FEVD, Blanchard-Quah, forecasts vs `vars`; bootstrap variants; edge cases and error messages |
| `test-bayes.R` | triangular sampler vs exact posterior, SV (Geweke), SSVS/horseshoe, fixed-hyperparameter NIW moments, Haar rotations, MC covariance, `mcmc_diagnostics` |
| `test-bvar-conj.R` | hierarchical NIW log posterior vs `BVAR`; sampler sanity; `irf`/`fevd`/`hd`/`forecast` on `bvarm` |
| `test-psvar.R` | proxy-SVAR vs hand computation, Mertens-Ravn B1, robust (MOSW) sets, block bootstrap, Bayesian proxy, LP-IV consistency |
| `test-psvar-bayes-full.R` | `varm_proxy_arw()` and `varm_proxy_gkr()` |
| `test-ident-extra.R` | `id_proxy`, `proxy_draws`, zero+sign, `id_restrictions`, `id_hetero` |
| `test-lp.R` | LP coefficients and HAC/HC errors vs `lm` + `sandwich`, LP-IV vs manual 2SLS |
| `test-lp-extra.R` | `lp_joint`, `lp_supt`, `lp_state` (vs `lm`+NW and `lpirfs`), `lp_smooth`, `lp_panel`, `lp_forecast`, `compare_lp_var` |
| `test-tvp.R` | dimensions, constant limit vs OLS, methods, variants, prior calibration |
| `test-methods.R` | print/summary/accessor methods, plotting |

## 2. Live checks: agreement with reference implementations

### 2.1 Reduced-form VAR against `vars`

```{r vars}
if (have("vars")) {
  f <- varm(Y, p = 2)
  v <- vars::VAR(Y, p = 2, type = "const")
  Bv <- sapply(v$varresult, coef)
  vs <- vars::VARselect(Y, lag.max = 6, type = "const")
  mine <- var_select(Y, 6)
  ir <- vars::irf(v, n.ahead = 12, ortho = TRUE, boot = FALSE)$irf
  fe <- vars::fevd(v, n.ahead = 13)
  m_ir <- irf(f, horizon = 12, ci = "none")$estimate
  m_fe <- fevd(f, horizon = 12, ci = "none")$estimate
  d_ir <- d_fe <- 0
  for (s in colnames(Y)) for (r in colnames(Y)) {
    d_ir <- max(d_ir, abs(unname(m_ir[r, s, ]) - ir[[s]][, r]))
    d_fe <- max(d_fe, abs(unname(m_fe[r, s, ]) - fe[[r]][, s]))
  }
  fc <- predict(v, n.ahead = 8, ci = 0.95)$fcst
  mf <- forecast(f, h = 8, ci = "none")$mean
  d_fc <- max(sapply(colnames(Y), function(k) max(abs(unname(mf[, k]) - fc[[k]][, "fcst"]))))
  res_vars <- tibble::tibble(
    quantity = c("coefficients B", "residual covariance", "log-likelihood", "information criteria (AIC, HQ, SC)",
                 "root moduli (companion)", "Cholesky IRF, h = 0..12", "FEVD, h = 0..12", "point forecast, h = 1..8"),
    max_abs_diff = c(max(abs(unname(f$B) - unname(Bv))),
                     max(abs(unname(f$Sigma) - unname(summary(v)$covres))),
                     abs(as.numeric(logLik(f)) - as.numeric(logLik(v))),
                     max(abs(unname(mine$criteria[, 1:3]) - unname(t(vs$criteria)[, 1:3]))),
                     max(abs(sort(stability(f), decreasing = TRUE) - sort(Mod(vars::roots(v)), decreasing = TRUE))),
                     d_ir, d_fe, d_fc))
  res_vars$max_abs_diff <- sci(res_vars$max_abs_diff)
  print(res_vars, n = Inf)
  cat("lag order chosen (AIC, HQ, SC, FPE): varm", mine$selection, "| vars", vs$selection, "\n")
}
```

The unit tests assert agreement to `1e-9`; the observed differences above are
rounding-level. Lag selection is identical (the information criteria differ by
rounding only).

### 2.2 Blanchard-Quah impact matrix against `vars::BQ`

```{r bq}
if (have("vars")) {
  bq <- vars::BQ(vars::VAR(Y[, 1:2], p = 2))
  P <- irf(varm(Y[, 1:2], p = 2), id = id_longrun(), horizon = 0, ci = "none")$estimate[, , 1]
  cat("max | |P_varm| - |P_vars| | =", sci(max(abs(abs(unname(P)) - abs(unname(bq$B))))), "(columns match up to sign)\n")
}
```

### 2.3 Local projections against `lm` + `sandwich`

For each response and horizon, LP is an OLS regression of $y_{t+h}$ on the
shock and controls. The comparison builds the same regression by hand with
`lm()` and takes the Newey-West (Bartlett, lag $h+1$, no prewhitening, no
small-sample factor) and HC1 variances from `sandwich`.

```{r lp-sandwich}
if (have("sandwich")) {
  n <- nrow(Y); p <- 3; H <- 6
  lead <- function(x, h) if (h == 0) x else c(x[-(1:h)], rep(NA, h))
  lagm <- function(x, l) c(rep(NA, l), x[1:(n - l)])
  dfL <- data.frame(Y)
  for (l in 1:p) for (v in colnames(Y)) dfL[[paste0(v, ".l", l)]] <- lagm(Y[, v], l)
  ctr <- paste(c("infl", "unemp", setdiff(names(dfL), colnames(Y))), collapse = "+")
  manual <- function(h, v) {
    d <- dfL; d$yy <- lead(Y[, v], h); d <- d[(p + 1):(n - h), ]
    lm(as.formula(paste("yy ~ rate +", ctr)), d)
  }
  f_nw <- lp(Y, shock = "rate", horizon = H, lags = p, contemp = c("infl", "unemp"))
  f_hc <- lp(Y, shock = "rate", horizon = H, lags = p, contemp = c("infl", "unemp"), se = "hc")
  d_b <- d_nw <- d_hc <- 0
  suppressWarnings(for (h in 0:H) for (v in colnames(Y)) {
    fm <- manual(h, v)
    d_b <- max(d_b, abs(f_nw$estimate[h + 1, v] - coef(fm)[["rate"]]))
    d_nw <- max(d_nw, abs(f_nw$se[h + 1, v] -
      sqrt(sandwich::NeweyWest(fm, lag = h + 1, prewhite = FALSE, adjust = FALSE)["rate", "rate"])))
    d_hc <- max(d_hc, abs(f_hc$se[h + 1, v] - sqrt(sandwich::vcovHC(fm, "HC1")["rate", "rate"])))
  })
  tibble::tibble(quantity = c("LP coefficient", "Newey-West se", "HC1 se"),
                 max_abs_diff = sci(c(d_b, d_nw, d_hc)), horizons = "0..6, all 3 responses")
}
```

### 2.4 State-dependent LP against `lpirfs::lp_nl`

`lp_state(timing = "lagged")` reproduces the `lpirfs` convention (logistic
state weight on the lagged HP-filtered indicator, interacted lag-1
coefficients, Cholesky columns of the linear VAR). One configuration is run
live; the second configuration (levels-standardised state, trend, a different
shock type) is in `validation/lp-extra.R`, and its output is quoted in section
3.4.

```{r lpirfs}
if (have("lpirfs")) {
  H <- 8; df <- as.data.frame(yraw)
  ref <- suppressMessages(lpirfs::lp_nl(df, lags_endog_lin = 2, lags_endog_nl = 2, trend = 0, shock_type = 0,
                       confint = 1, hor = H, switching = yraw$infl, use_hp = 1, lambda = 1600,
                       gamma = 3, use_nw = TRUE, num_cores = 1))
  d <- sapply(1:3, function(sj) {
    me <- lp_state(yraw, all_of(sj), "infl", H, lags = 2, timing = "lagged", lags_lin = 2, shock_type = 0,
                   gamma = 3, hp_lambda = 1600, state_const = FALSE, trend = FALSE)
    c(high = max(abs(me$estimate[, , "high"] - t(ref$irf_s1_mean[, , sj]))),
      low = max(abs(me$estimate[, , "low"] - t(ref$irf_s2_mean[, , sj]))))
  })
  colnames(d) <- paste("shock", 1:3)
  apply(d, 1:2, sci)
}
```

### 2.5 Hierarchical Bayesian VAR: log posterior against `BVAR`

`BVAR::bvar()` optimises the log posterior of the hyperparameters
$(\lambda, \mu, \theta, \psi)$ (overall tightness, sum-of-coefficients,
single-unit-root, prior scale). Evaluating the `varm` log posterior at the same
point (with the same `psi` and the same hyperprior parameters) must give the
same value. The comparison is deterministic, so any difference is numerical
rounding. It uses internal helper functions (`varm:::cpp_niw_logpost`).

```{r bvar-logpost}
if (have("BVAR")) {
  p <- 4
  set.seed(1)
  bv <- suppressWarnings(BVAR::bvar(Y, lags = p, n_draw = 400, n_burn = 100, n_thin = 1,
        priors = BVAR::bv_priors(hyper = "auto", mn = BVAR::bv_mn(), soc = BVAR::bv_soc(), sur = BVAR::bv_sur()),
        verbose = FALSE))
  ols <- varm:::cpp_var_ols(Y, p, matrix(1, nrow(Y), 1))
  b <- matrix(0, 13, 3); b[cbind(1:3, 1:3)] <- 1
  gamma_coef <- varm:::gamma_coef
  gp <- rbind(gamma_coef(.2, .4), gamma_coef(2, .25), gamma_coef(1, 1), gamma_coef(1, 1))
  h <- c(bv$optim$par[["lambda"]], 2, bv$optim$par[["soc"]], bv$optim$par[["sur"]], bv$priors$psi$mode)
  v <- varm:::cpp_niw_logpost(h, ols$Y, ols$X, p, 1L, TRUE, b, 1e7, c(1L, 0L, 1L, 1L, 0L, 0L, 0L), gp,
                              c(1e-4, 1, 1e-4, 1e-4, 0, 0, 0), c(5, 3, 50, 50, Inf, Inf, Inf), c(.004, .004), FALSE)
  cat(sprintf("log posterior: BVAR %.10f  varm %.10f  |diff| = %s (relative %s)\n",
              bv$optim$value, v, sci(abs(v - bv$optim$value)), sci(abs(v - bv$optim$value) / abs(v))))
}
```

### 2.6 Draw-based IRFs: consistency of the three uncertainty engines

There is no external reference for the *bands*, so this check is internal:
the bootstrap, the asymptotic Monte Carlo and the Bayesian sampler should
produce bands of similar width for the same data when the Bayesian prior is
loose. This is a consistency check, not a proof of correctness.

```{r draws-consistency, fig.height = 3}
set.seed(11)
f <- varm(Y, p = 2)
b_boot <- irf(f, id = id_chol(), horizon = 12, ci = "bootstrap", nboot = 1000)
b_mc   <- irf(f, id = id_chol(), horizon = 12, ci = "mc", nboot = 1000)
bf <- bvarm(Y, p = 2, prior_minnesota(lambda = c(5, 1, 1e-4, 50), soc = NULL, sur = NULL, hyper = character(0)),
            ndraw = 1000)
b_bay <- irf(bf, id = id_chol(), horizon = 12)

# one tidy() frame per engine: response of unemp to a rate shock, 90% band
cell <- function(ir, engine) {
  d <- tidy(ir)
  d <- d[d$response == "unemp" & d$shock == "rate" & d$level == 0.9, ]
  d$engine <- engine
  d
}
d <- rbind(cell(b_boot, "bootstrap"), cell(b_mc, "asymptotic MC"), cell(b_bay, "loose BVAR"))
aggregate(cbind(width = conf.high - conf.low) ~ engine, data = d, FUN = mean) |>
  transform(width = round(width, 3))
ggplot(d, aes(horizon, estimate, colour = engine, fill = engine)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = varm_palette(3)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = varm_palette(3)) +
  labs(x = "Horizon (quarters)", y = "Response of unemp to rate", colour = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_varm()
```

(Mean width of the 90% band of the response of `unemp` to `rate`, horizons 0
to 12, and the bands themselves.)

### 2.7 The tidy layer is a lossless view of the objects

`tidy()`, `glance()` and `autoplot()` are thin layers over the stored arrays;
the unit tests cover them. Live, the tibbles reproduce the internals exactly
and every plot builds:

```{r tidy-layer}
f <- varm(Y, p = 2)
ir <- irf(f, id = id_chol(), horizon = 12, ci = "none")
td <- tidy(ir)
lpf <- lp(Y, shock = rate, contemp = c(infl, unemp), horizon = 6, lags = 2)
tl <- tidy(lpf, conf.int = FALSE)
tibble::tibble(
  check = c("tidy(varm) vs coef()", "tidy(irf) vs $estimate", "tidy(lp) vs $estimate"),
  max_abs_diff = sci(c(
    max(abs(tidy(f)$estimate - as.vector(coef(f)))),
    max(abs(td$estimate - ir$estimate[cbind(as.integer(td$response), as.integer(td$shock), td$horizon + 1)])),
    max(abs(tl$estimate - lpf$estimate[cbind(tl$horizon + 1, as.integer(tl$response))]))
  ))
)
glance(f)
inherits(autoplot(ir), "ggplot") && inherits(autoplot(lpf), "ggplot")
```

## 3. Quoted results of the longer scripts

Each block shows the output of the stated command. They are not recomputed when
the vignette is built.

### 3.1 Bayesian engines: `Rscript validation/bayes.R`

**Triangular sampler against an exact posterior (s1).** With homoskedastic
errors the triangular prior is semi-conjugate, so the posterior of each
equation has a one-dimensional-quadrature form. The sampler's draws are
compared with it by $z$-scores of posterior means and variance ratios.

```text
[PASS] 1a K=1 matches exact semi-conjugate posterior  max|z|= 2.22  var ratio range 0.997-1.018
[PASS] 1b K=3 reduced-form (B, Sigma, A) vs exact structural posterior  max|z| B/Sigma/A: 1.61 1.52 1.59
[PASS] 1c loose prior reproduces OLS  max|B-OLS|= 0.00121  (Sigma mean rel dev  0.066 )
```

**Stochastic volatility (s2).** The Kim-Shephard-Chib mixture is an
approximation of the $\log\chi^2_1$ density, so the Geweke joint-distribution
test is run with tolerance $|z|<4$ rather than 2.

```text
Geweke z (sig2,h0,hT,mean h): 0.61 -1.05 -0.94 -0.99  var ratios: 1.002 0.998 0.999 0.998
[PASS] 2a Geweke joint-distribution test (KSC approx; mixture is approximate, tolerance |z|<4)
eq1 (tv): cor(h)=0.965 90% coverage=0.82 ; sigma_h posterior mean=0.084 (true 0.12)
eq2 (const): 90% coverage=0.98 ; mean sd of h2 path=0.234; sigma_h mean=0.074 (true 0, prior mean 0.1)
[PASS] 2b time-varying vol recovery
[PASS] 2b constant vol recovered (sigma_h shrinks, coverage)
[PASS] 2c Sigma = A^-1 Lambda A^-T algebra (last-period vol)  max err 0
```

Note the 90% credible band of the true volatility path covers 82% in the
time-varying equation, and the posterior mean of the volatility-of-volatility
$\sigma_h$ is 0.084 against a truth of 0.12 (one dataset).

**Simulation-based calibration of $\sigma_h^2$ (s2d).** Truths are drawn from
the prior, data are simulated, and the 90% credible interval of $\sigma_h^2$ and
of the log-volatility path are checked (60 replications):

```text
rank histogram (quintiles) of true sigma_h^2 in posterior: 6 9 14 13 18
[PASS] 2d sigma_h^2 90% credible-interval coverage (prior-drawn truths)  cov= 0.833  mean vol-path 90% coverage= 0.883
```

The coverage of $\sigma_h^2$ is 0.83 against a nominal 0.90, and the rank
histogram is tilted toward high ranks (true value ranked high in the posterior,
i.e. the posterior of $\sigma_h^2$ is a little too low). With 60 replications
the standard error of a coverage estimate is about 0.04, so the shortfall is
suggestive rather than conclusive; see section 5.

**Shrinkage priors (s3).**

```text
[PASS] 3a SSVS inclusion separates true nonzeros from zeros  P(incl|nonzero)= 0.903  P(incl|zero)= 0.199
[PASS] 3b horseshoe/SSVS beat OLS RMSE; horseshoe shrinks zeros  rmse hs/ssvs/ols= 0.0362 0.0351 0.0717
```

**Conjugate NIW sampler (s4).** Fixed hyperparameters: draws against the
analytic NIW moments. Hierarchical: posterior means of the hyperparameters
against an exact quadrature, and against `BVAR`'s own MCMC.

```text
[PASS] 4a fixed-hyper draws vs analytic ...  z= 3.26  Sigma rel= 0.0013  var rel= 0.0155  corr maxdiff= 0.0134
      lambda    soc    sur
varm  0.9747 0.3682 0.6843
BVAR  0.9869 0.3652 0.6107
exact 0.9800 0.3749 0.6651
[PASS] 4b hierarchical hyper means: varm MCMC vs exact quadrature (within 5%)  rel diffs 0.005 0.018 0.029 | BVAR's own MCMC vs exact: 0.007 0.026 0.082
[PASS] 4c posterior mean of B vs BVAR   max |posterior mean B diff| = 0.00516
```

The max $z$ of 3.26 (over all coefficients; the script's threshold is 4.5) is
the weakest of the agreement numbers in this block. The draws are iid here, so
this is a single large-ish order statistic rather than evidence of autocorrelation,
but it is the number to look at if the fixed-hyperparameter sampler is ever
changed.

**Sign restrictions and Haar rotations (s5).**

```text
[PASS] 5a Haar K=2: orthogonal, entry law exact (KS), E[Q^2]=1/K, E[det]=0  KS= 0.00195 0.00147  E[Q^2] range 0.4996-0.5004  E[det]= 4e-04
[PASS] 5a Haar K=3: ...  KS= 0.00144 0.00286  E[Q^2] range 0.3326-0.3341  E[det]= -0.002
[PASS] 5b K=2 demand/supply toy: acceptance = 1/2  acc= 0.5011
[PASS] 5b accepted demand-shock angles confined to (0,pi/2) and uniform there  KS= 0.00204
[PASS] 5b K=3 fully signed column: acceptance = 1/4  acc= 0.2507
[PASS] 5b K=3 two restricted columns vs independent R Haar sampler  C++: 0.1678 R: 0.1656
[PASS] 5c accepted IRFs satisfy all sign restrictions; P P' = Sigma  violations= 0  of  202500  max|PP'-Sigma|= 6.7e-16  acceptance rate= 0.0704  accepted draws= 2500
```

**MCMC diagnostics (s7).** `mcmc_diagnostics()` is tested on AR(1) chains with
known effective sample size $n(1-\phi)/(1+\phi)$:

```text
[PASS] 7a ESS of AR(1) phi=.8 vs theory n(1-phi)/(1+phi)  mean ESS= 449  theory= 444
[PASS] 7b multi-chain: converged chains R-hat ~ 1, ESS(iid) ~ N
[PASS] 7c non-mixed chains detected by R-hat  rhat= 2.27
[PASS] 7d Geweke z ~ N(0,1) under stationarity (sd in 0.8-1.25), large under drift  sd(z)= 1.02  drift z= -21.1
```

### 3.2 Coverage of draw-based IRF bands (s6)

Design: Cholesky IRFs of a bivariate VAR(1), $T=200$, 300 replications, 400
draws each, averaged over the $2\times2\times13$ responses; "bc" is Kilian
bias correction. The persistence is $\rho=0.9$.

```text
IRF coverage, iid errors
  method cov68 cov90   w68   w90
     iid 0.593 0.809 0.128 0.211
  iid_bc 0.674 0.893 0.156 0.256
    wild 0.552 0.754 0.120 0.196
 wild_bc 0.622 0.831 0.146 0.239
      mc 0.653 0.876 0.136 0.231

IRF coverage, heteroskedastic errors
  method cov68 cov90   w68   w90
     iid 0.475 0.701 0.210 0.345
  iid_bc 0.385 0.610 0.254 0.419
    wild 0.531 0.753 0.223 0.365
 wild_bc 0.437 0.655 0.283 0.461
      mc 0.420 0.614 0.218 0.370
```

What these numbers say:

* With persistent data ($\rho=0.9$) and $T=200$, only the bias-corrected iid
  bootstrap (0.893) and the Monte Carlo (0.876) are close to the nominal 90%.
  The plain iid bootstrap covers 81%, the plain wild bootstrap 75%.
* Under heteroskedasticity every method under-covers; the wild bootstrap
  (0.753) is the best of them but still 15 points below nominal. The
  bias-corrected versions are *worse* there (0.61-0.66).
* The script's pass criteria are relative ("within 0.07 of nominal" for the iid
  design with the chosen methods; "wild at least as good as iid" for the
  heteroskedastic one), which is weaker than "nominal coverage achieved".

```text
 mosw    8   0.785  0.0291               mosw    8   0.910  Inf
```

(The two panels were reformatted from the script's output; `mosw` is the
Montiel Olea-Stock-Watson robust set from `varm_proxy_robust()`.)

Coverage of the two newer Bayesian proxy-SVAR samplers (`varm_proxy_arw()`,
`varm_proxy_gkr()`), $K=3$ VAR(1), $T=300$, 50 replications
(`Rscript validation/proxy-bayes-full.R`; with 50 replications a coverage
estimate has a standard error of about 0.04 to 0.07):

```text
 arw68  arw90  gkr_set  gkr_rcr  gkr_bayes90  w_rcr  w_bayes
 0.690  0.910  0.573    0.907    0.647        0.852  0.708
```

`arw68`/`arw90` are the coverages of the 68% and 90% posterior bands for the
impact responses to the proxied shock. For the set-identified shock,
`gkr_set` is how often the truth lies inside the estimated set of posterior
means (0.57, so the set of posterior means alone is not a confidence set),
`gkr_rcr` is the coverage of the 90% robust credible region (0.91) and
`gkr_bayes90` that of the conventional single-prior 90% band (0.65); `w_rcr`
and `w_bayes` are the mean widths (0.85 against 0.71).

## 4. Timing

All numbers are seconds of elapsed time on an Apple M4 Pro (R 4.6.1, OpenBLAS,
single-threaded with `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1`, nothing else running), with the installed
package. Reproduce the Bayesian block
with `Rscript validation/bayes.R s8` (its DGP: $T=250$, $p=4$, 1000 retained
draws; the numbers below come from the installed package, `s8` through
`pkgload::load_all()` gave the same values to within about 0.2 s except the
hierarchical $K=3$ row, 0.12 s against 0.08 s).

| seconds per 1000 draws | K = 3 | K = 7 | K = 20 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bvarm`, conjugate, fixed hyperparameters | 0.003 | 0.010 | 0.061 |
| `bvarm`, conjugate, hierarchical (optimiser + MH, 500 burn-in) | 0.054 | 0.177 | 1.271 |
| `bvarm`, triangular Minnesota, homoskedastic (200 burn-in) | 0.019 | 0.110 | 1.312 |
| `bvarm`, triangular horseshoe, homoskedastic | 0.05 | 0.28 | 5.92 |
| `bvarm`, triangular Minnesota + stochastic volatility | 0.112 | 0.382 | 2.979 |
| `BVAR::bvar` (hierarchical $\lambda$) | 0.157 | 0.259 | 0.899 |
| `bsvars::bsvar_sv` (structural SV, $S=1000$) | 1.35 | 4.64 | not run |

Honest reading, comparing the hierarchical conjugate sampler with
`BVAR::bvar` (the closest like-for-like): `varm` is about three times as fast at
$K=3$ (0.054 against 0.157 s), faster at $K=7$ (0.177 against 0.259 s) and
**slower at $K=20$** (1.27 against 0.90 s). The two samplers are not identical
(`varm` also runs an optimiser before the Metropolis chain; the triangular
and SV samplers have no `BVAR` counterpart, and `BVAR::bvar` is at 0.157 s for
$K=3$ against 0.112 s for `varm` with SV, which is a different model). The $K=20$ timing was identical with
`OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1`, so it is not a threading artefact. Other models on
`yraw` ($T=215$, $K=3$, $p=2$):

* `tvpvar()` with SV, time-varying $A_t$ and full $Q$, 10000 draws and 2000
  burn-in sweeps ($T=215$, $K=3$, $p=2$; estimation sample 173): about 8 s on an
  otherwise idle machine. Timings taken while other jobs were running were up to
  four times higher, so quote them only from a quiet machine. Cost grows with $p$.
* A full 3-variable `lp()` (17 horizons, 3 responses): about 0.5 ms per call;
  `varm()` OLS about 0.05 ms. One thousand wild-bootstrap draws of a VAR(2):
  0.02 s; the IRF with wild bands (1000 draws, 17 horizons): 0.03 s. (Best of
  three runs on an Apple M4 Pro with `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1`.)

## 5. Failures and limitations found

These are the findings of the checks above that a user should know about.

1. **Proxy-SVAR wild bootstrap does not cover the normalised impact response.**
   In `validation/proxy-coverage.R`, the wild-bootstrap 90% interval for the
   impact response ($h=0$) covers 13.5% (strong instrument) and 21% (weak
   instrument) of the time, and 0.15 in `ident-extra.R`. The interval is
   very narrow (median width 0.027 against 0.20 for the block bootstrap); the
   cause was not investigated here. Use `type = "mbb"` (moving block bootstrap, Jentsch and
   Lunsford) or `varm_proxy_robust()`. At horizons 1 to 8 the wild bootstrap
   covers 81-85% (strong instrument), still below nominal. The moving-block
   bootstrap covers 77-87% with a strong instrument, i.e. under-covers
   somewhat at this $T$.
2. **Weak-instrument robust sets are infinite, as they should be.** With
   median $F=2$ the MOSW sets have infinite width and cover 88-94%; the bootstrap
   intervals have finite width but the moving-block one is very wide at $h=0$
   (3.76) and its coverage is 0.86-0.945.
3. **Stochastic-volatility calibration is slightly under-covering.** The
   volatility-of-volatility interval covers 83% (nominal 90%, 60 replications)
   and the time-varying-equation path covers 82%; the posterior of $\sigma_h$
   tends to be low (0.084 against 0.12). The Kim-Shephard-Chib mixture is itself
   an approximation (Geweke test needs tolerance $|z|<4$).
4. **Bootstrap coverage under persistence and heteroskedasticity.** With
   $\rho=0.9$, $T=200$ the plain bootstrap covers 75-81% at the 90% level, and
   under heteroskedastic errors every draw-based method covers 61-75%; Kilian's
   bias correction helps with iid errors and hurts with heteroskedastic errors
   (section 3.2). Treat 90% bands from a short, persistent, heteroskedastic
   sample as approximately 70-75% bands.
5. **Sup-t bands under-cover in the simulation.** Whole-path coverage is 0.78
   with HAC errors and 0.84 with lag-augmented HC errors, against a nominal
   0.90, but the pointwise band covers the whole path only 24% of the time, so
   the sup-t adjustment is a large improvement though not complete. The
   shortfall is the finite-sample undercoverage of HAC/HC errors carried over.
6. **Hierarchical NIW sampler mixes slowly.** `mcmc_diagnostics()` on a
   `bvarm` fit of `yraw` with 3000 retained draws and 1000 burn-in (one
   chain) reported effective sample sizes of about 158 ($\lambda$), 72
   (soc) and 89 (sur) (split R-hat 1.00-1.01), against 3000 draws. Run several chains or increase `ndraw` when you need tail
   probabilities of the hyperparameters. The posterior means agree with the
   exact quadrature to 0.5-3% (section 3.1).
7. **TVP-VAR path coverage depends on the prior.** When the data are generated
   from the sampler's own prior, 90% bands cover 0.91/0.94/0.89 (beta, $A$,
   log-volatility). When the data come from a simulated TVP-SV process
   ($T=250$, $K=3$) and the sampler uses the data-driven training-sample prior,
   coverage depends on the prior tightness $k_Q$: with the default $k_Q=0.01$
   the coefficient bands cover 56% and the log-variance bands 65% (8
   replications, so large uncertainty); with $k_Q=0.05$ it is 79% and 68%.
   Choose `tvp_prior(kQ = )` with care and check the sensitivity.
8. **Speed claims are specific to the machine and the settings** (section 4).
   `BVAR::bvar` is faster at $K=20$.

## 6. What has *not* been validated

* The Bayesian proxy-SVAR variants (`varm_proxy_bayes()`, `varm_proxy_arw()`,
  `varm_proxy_gkr()`) are checked for internal consistency, against the
  bootstrap with a strong proxy (`varm_proxy_bayes()`) and by the coverage
  simulation in section 3.3; there is no comparison with a published
  replication.
* `lp_panel()` is checked against `lm` with dummy variables and hand-coded
  cluster errors on an unbalanced panel, not against `plm` or `fixest`.
* `id_hetero()` recovers the impact matrix in a two-regime simulation; there
  is no external reference implementation compared.
* `forecast()` is checked for the point forecast against `vars`; density
  forecasts and `hd()` are not compared with another package.
* Missing values are rejected with an error (not handled), and nothing here
  covers VARs larger than $K=20$.
